content.text:
Nature and science facts about the rhino

A rhino's big horn is not bone — it's made of keratin, the same stuff as our hair and nails, so it can grow and wear down. Its thick, tough skin is like armor. The rhino is a plant-eater that feeds on grass and leaves, and although its eyesight isn't very sharp, it has an excellent sense of smell and hearing. On hot days it takes mud baths to protect its skin, and sadly, poaching for its horn has left it endangered, so it needs our protection.

Great points to observe together

Point out things like the horn (keratin), the thick skin, the keen sense of smell and hearing, and its endangered status. Talking through "What is a rhino's horn made of?" together is a lovely way to explore.

content.text:
Parent guide — nurturing curiosity

Try comparing "the horn is made of the same stuff as your nails" with your child's own fingernails. Compare mud baths to a hippo, and talking about "the horn is what puts it in danger (so it needs protecting)" helps grow a caring heart for living things.

content.text:
Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)

Q. What is a rhino's horn made of?
A. Not bone, but keratin — the same material as our hair and nails. It can grow and wear down.

Q. Why does the rhino need protection?
A. Because poaching for its horn has left it endangered.

Q. How can we observe at home?
A. Comparing your nails to the horn's material, and comparing mud baths to a hippo, both work well.
